findings: Fail-open guarantee rests on an oracle return contract the plan never confirms: The plan treats the 8f6c facade's 'three-valued abstain-by-default contract' as the whole fail-open guarantee for the only blocking tier. It names no return type, no abstain variant and no file:symbol. The three facade functions do exist, but I could not find any abstain or verdict type in rebar.grounding, and the prerequisite ticket cannot be loaded to check the contract. If the oracle raises an exception on a timeout or a missing binary, or returns two-valued results, the DET floor would fail closed and wrongly block tickets on unsupported stacks. That breaks the 'ironclad' promise.

No mapping from P2/P3/P4 to facade calls, and abstain-as-PASS hides broken wiring: The plan says P2/P3/P4 are consumed through 'refute_absence/applies/scan' but never says which call serves which check. It also never confirms that the facade exposes ctags symbol resolution, deps.dev plus optional syft package existence, and scc/lizard oversize metrics. Because abstain means PASS, a check whose capability the facade lacks would pass silently on every input, and the only blocking tier would claim coverage it does not have. The ACs only test fail-open. Nothing tests that a check actually fires on a supported stack.

'Only blocking tier' claim contradicts the opt-in LLM blocking AC: The Why section says outright that the DET floor is the ONLY blocking tier and that every LLM criterion is advisory. The third AC says LLM criteria can block through an opt-in `block_threshold`, and that DET-only is just a default posture, 'not an architectural limit'. Both cannot be true. An implementer could not tell whether to build or preserve a per-criterion LLM blocking path, or to rely on the DET floor being the sole gate.

P3 live registry lookup conflicts with the 'frozen, deterministic' floor: The floor must be 'frozen, deterministic', but P3 checks package existence against the live deps.dev registry. The registry's answers change as packages are published or yanked, and network failures or timeouts turn into abstain=PASS. The same ticket can therefore get different blocking verdicts on different runs or machines, and offline runs silently lose P3.

P8 token estimator and 'largest configured context window' are undefined: P8 is a blocking DET check, but the plan names no token estimator (an offline heuristic or a provider count API), no error margin, no rule for near-threshold cases, and no config source for 'the largest configured context window'. An exact Claude count needs a network API, which is not deterministic or offline. A heuristic can produce false blocking FAILs. 'Or is anticipated to exceed' is also unspecified, so the check cannot be built or tested without clarification.

No edit set: new modules, orchestrator dispatch and attestation field are unnamed: The plan adds P1, P5, P6, P7 and P8, the P2/P3/P4 wiring, an exec=DET dispatch path in the orchestrator's code executor, and a coverage field on the attestation. It names no file, module or symbol for any of these. None of the likely homes resolve (rebar.review, rebar.orchestrator, rebar.plan_review, rebar.attestation). So it is unclear whether the orchestrator executor, the attestation schema and the 'size-handling ladder' already exist or must be built. The plan also does not say that the shared src/rebar/grounding/, which code-review 9da1 also uses, must stay read-only.

Deterministic P6/P7 semantics and 'escalates T4' are unspecified: P6 ('AC/DD quality') and P7 ('destructive/irreversible sniff (escalates T4)') are blocking DET checks with no definition of what they detect, what rules or patterns they use, or what 'escalates T4' means in practice: emit a finding, change a tier, or block. Judging AC quality deterministically is not obvious, and an implementer would have to invent the rules. Blocking checks built on guessed rules risk false blocks.

Title does not describe the work: The plan title is 'engine comparison', but the body builds the DET blocking floor (P1–P8 and the exec=DET path) and compares no engines. Anyone triaging by title, and any intent-fidelity check, would be misled.

The rebar-owned checks P1 'readiness-shape', P5 'interference', P6 'AC/DD quality' and P7 'destructive/irreversible sniff' are named but never defined. The plan does not say what rule each one evaluates, what input it reads, or what makes it pass or fail. An executor cannot implement them without asking.

'P7 … (escalates T4)' does not say what 'escalate' means. Does P7 fail/block in the DET floor, only raise an advisory flag, or force the T4 overlay to run? The phrase 'sniff' suggests a heuristic, yet P7 sits in the only blocking tier.

P7 is a 'destructive/irreversible sniff' that 'escalates T4', but it sits in the DET floor, which is the only tier that blocks by default. The plan doesn't say whether a P7 hit blocks, only escalates or routes to T4, or both. A lexical sniff that blocks outright would produce false-positive blocks, which this floor is meant to avoid.

Every test-related AC exercises only the abstain/skipped=PASS path. No AC requires any check to FAIL on a known-bad input or to PASS cleanly on a known-good one. A floor whose checks always abstain or always pass would satisfy every acceptance criterion, even though this is the only blocking tier.

Observation on sequencing and size: the unit bundles eight checks plus a new first-class exec=DET dispatch path, and gives no order or thin first slice. The riskiest piece is the new execution path plus facade wiring. Nothing says it is proven end-to-end with one check before the remaining checks are layered on, and the whole may not fit one session as a leaf.

P8 depends on a derived metric with no computation protocol. The plan does not define the token-estimate method (tokenizer or chars/N heuristic), where the 'largest configured context window' is read from, or what a 'parent+child pairing for container criteria' includes.

The plan gives P8 two different execution paths. The P8 section says 'the orchestrator emits it during the size-handling ladder'. The T8 AC says 'P1–P8 run as the deterministic exec=DET tier the orchestrator dispatches via its code executor'. The plan doesn't settle which component owns P8, when it runs relative to the size ladder and LLM dispatch, or how to prevent duplicate or conflicting P8 findings.

P8's execution path is stated two ways. One says 'the orchestrator emits it during the size-handling ladder'. The T8 AC says P1–P8 are dispatched uniformly as the exec=DET tier via the code executor. It is unclear whether P8 is a DET-floor check or an orchestrator-ladder emission.

The Why requires a 'frozen, deterministic' floor, but P3 depends on a live deps.dev registry lookup. Its answer can change over time (packages published or yanked), and network flakiness turns it into abstain=PASS. The same ticket can therefore get different blocking verdicts on different runs.

P8's execution site is stated two ways. The P8 section says 'the orchestrator emits it during the size-handling ladder'. The T8 AC says P1–P8 all run as the exec=DET tier dispatched via the code executor. It is unclear which path produces the P8 finding, or whether both do, which risks duplicate or missing findings.

P3 (package existence) checks the live deps.dev registry, and network timeouts abstain to PASS. That contradicts the stated goal of a 'frozen, deterministic' blocking floor. The same ticket can pass on one run (timeout -> abstain) and fail on another, and a package that doesn't exist today can later be registered (for example by a squatter), which flips the verdict. The plan doesn't pin, snapshot or record the registry answer.

P8's threshold isn't defined well enough to be deterministic. It depends on an unspecified 'token-estimate' and on 'the largest configured context window', which is LLM configuration. So whether this blocking DET check fails depends on which estimator and which model config are active, and neither is recorded. Changing the model config silently changes what blocks.

P8 is a blocking DET check, but its fail-open behaviour is unspecified. The fail-open AC covers only P1–P7. Nothing says what happens if the token estimator errors, or if the 'largest configured context window' config is missing or malformed.
The title 'engine comparison 012e-bd01-75c6-40a3' does not describe the body, which is the DET-floor implementation. This is a title/body conflicting signal.
The plan title 'engine comparison 012e-bd01-75c6-40a3' does not describe the work. The body builds the DET blocking floor (P1–P8 plus the exec=DET path) and compares no engines.

No edit set, and the Phase 1 dependency isn't cited or present in the repo: The plan names no files, modules or symbols for the batch assembler, the single CI trigger or the atomic-submit path. Its only prerequisite is an uncited 'Phase 1'. The repository has no Autosubmit queue, CI-trigger or submit code to extend, so the edit targets, the blast radius and the dependency can't be checked. An implementer also can't tell whether to extend existing serial per-change code or build something new.

The '~3 concurrent runs' Free-tier GHA cap is unsourced and appears wrong, and AC4 depends on it: The Why section and AC4 both rest on a '~3 concurrent runs' Free-tier cap. GitHub-hosted Free plans limit concurrent jobs (20 on standard runners), not runs, to roughly 3. If the real constraint is a repo-level `concurrency:` group or a different limit, both the batching rationale and the batch-size bound are miscalibrated. Nothing in the repo (no workflow files) backs the figure.

Atomic land isn't guaranteed: no re-validation between assembly/CI and submit: AC3 requires 'the tested tip == the landed tree'. CI takes a full cycle, and during it main can advance or a member change can get a new patchset or lose votes. The plan has no compare-and-set before submitting: checking that main still equals the batch base and that each member is still at its tested patchset. Without that, the submit can land an untested tree or fail partway.

Ancestor-atomic submit depends on Verified-casting, which the plan scopes out: A Gerrit submit of a relation-chain tip only lands ancestors that are each submittable (Verified and Code-Review satisfied on every change). The plan says 'Verified-casting ... [is a] separate story', but AC3 (atomic submit on green) can't pass unless something casts Verified on every member from the single combined CI run. The AC is either unsatisfiable inside this phase's scope or quietly depends on an uncited sibling.

Rebasing into a combined chain creates new patchsets, and vote carry-over isn't addressed: To put independent changes and stacks into one linear chain on current main, every member except possibly the first has to be rebased onto a new parent, which creates new patchsets. Whether Code-Review and other votes survive depends on the project's label copyCondition. If they don't carry over, nothing in the chain is submittable after assembly. The plan doesn't mention this integration constraint.

Assembly conflicts and the batch-failure path are undefined: Combining independent stacks can produce rebase conflicts during assembly, before any CI run, and the plan doesn't say what happens then (drop the conflicting stack, abort the batch, fall back to serial). Batch-failure handling is deferred, so in this phase a red combined run lands nothing and leaves the queue in an undefined state. That also undermines the 'wall-clock-optimal' claim, since one bad change blocks all N.

No testing plan or verifiable evidence for the ACs: The plan has no tests or verification steps. Several ACs need concrete evidence to be checkable: 'exactly ONE CI run', 'tested tip == landed tree', and the documented bound. Nothing says how those will be shown (a mocked Gerrit/GHA integration test, a dry-run against a sandbox project, or something else).

The batch-size bound in AC4 is ambiguous: 'Bounded to one CI run's job budget' doesn't say how batch size maps to CI jobs. A single run on the combined tip usually runs the same job matrix however many changes are in it, so the bound as written has no clear metric. Without a defined number (or formula) and where it's configured, AC4 can't be verified.

How the single CI run is triggered isn't specified: The plan says it triggers CI once on a Gerrit relation-chain tip, while CI is GitHub Actions. It doesn't say how the combined tip reaches GHA (mirror push to a ref, workflow_dispatch, or something else), which workflow runs, or how the existing per-change triggers are kept from also firing on each rebased patchset. If they do fire, 'exactly ONE CI run' is broken.

No rollout or rollback switch from the serial path: Batching replaces the Phase 1 serial land path but has no feature flag, kill switch or fallback to serial mode. If batching misbehaves (stuck queue, a bad atomic land), there's no documented way to go back.

The title doesn't describe the deliverable: The plan is titled 'engine comparison', but the content is a Phase 2 implementation of batched Autosubmit landing. The mismatch makes it harder to trace and to link with sibling phases.

AC3 assumes Gerrit gives 'ancestor-atomic submit' and that 'the tested tip == the landed tree', without checking either. Gerrit's docs show that under Merge If Necessary (the default) or Rebase If Necessary, a submit made after main has moved creates a merge commit or rebases. The landed tree then differs from the CI-tested tip. Gerrit's own design talk describes ancestor submission as 'pseudo atomic'.

The plan claims 'the tested tip == the landed tree', but that only holds under certain project submit types and only if main has not moved during CI. With MERGE_IF_NECESSARY, REBASE_IF_NECESSARY/ALWAYS or CHERRY_PICK, a main that advanced during the CI run lands a tree that was never tested. The plan states no submit type and no guard against main moving.

'The tested tip == the landed tree' is under-specified for the case where `main` advances between the CI trigger and the submit. The plan names no Gerrit submit type, and no behaviour when the base moves. Under Rebase-If-Necessary or Cherry-Pick submit types the landed tree can differ from the tested tree.

The plan's rationale and AC4 rest on the premise that the Free-tier GHA concurrency cap is about 3 concurrent runs. Nothing backs this: the repo has no workflow, runner or concurrency config (no .github/ directory), and the plan cites no source. GitHub's published Free-plan limit is per concurrent JOB (about 20, with 5 on macOS), not about 3 runs, so the premise may be wrong or may reflect a repo-specific `concurrency:` setting that does not exist yet.

AC3 asserts that ancestor-atomic submit makes the tested tip equal the landed tree. That only holds under certain Gerrit project submit types (for example Fast Forward Only, or Merge If Necessary with the chain already on the current main tip) and if main does not move between the CI run and submit. With Rebase Always or Cherry Pick, Gerrit creates new commits at submit time. The plan names no submit-type setting, and the repo has no Gerrit config or integration to confirm one.

The atomic-land mechanism has a check-then-act race. The chain is built on 'current main', CI runs for a full cycle, then the tip is submitted. The plan never requires re-checking that main still equals the assembly base, or that every member is unchanged (no new patchset, not abandoned, votes still present), right before submit. If main moves, Gerrit's merge-if-necessary or rebase-if-necessary submit types will silently produce a tree CI never tested. That breaks the AC 'the tested tip == the landed tree'.

The batch-size bound is tied to the wrong resource. Batching triggers ONE CI run on the combined tip, so batch size does not change the number of concurrent runs counted against the GHA cap of about 3. Unless the CI fans out per change, it does not change a single run's job count either. The real limits on batch size are the chance that one bad change fails the whole batch and the cost of isolating it, plus assembly conflict probability. As written, the AC asks the implementer to derive the bound from a constraint the bound does not actually affect.

The plan's main constraint, 'Free-tier GHA concurrency cap (~3 concurrent runs)', is unverified and contradicts current sources. GitHub Free allows 20 concurrent jobs on standard hosted runners, and none of the retrieved sources mention a 3-run cap. Both the case against speculation and the AC4 batch-size bound are built on this number.

The plan's rationale and AC4 rest on a 'Free-tier GHA concurrency cap (~3 concurrent runs)'. That figure is asserted without a source and should not be trusted from training knowledge, which recalls Free-plan limits as counted in concurrent jobs (around 20, with a smaller macOS limit) rather than ~3 runs. AC4 also ties batch size to 'one CI run's job budget', but the number of jobs in a single run on the combined tip doesn't grow with batch size. The constraint the bound is supposed to enforce is therefore unclear.

The plan never defines how queued changes are selected and ordered into the combined chain. It does not say what 'queued' means (Autosubmit+1 vote? a label? also requiring Code-Review+2?). It does not say how independent stacks are ordered relative to each other (FIFO by vote time? priority?). It does not say what happens to stacks that exceed the batch bound.

The batch-size bound conflates two different limits and asserts a number without deriving it. The Why section reasons about a cap on concurrent runs (~3). AC4 bounds the batch by 'one CI run's job budget' but says it 'fits the GHA concurrency cap'. A single run's job count and the number of concurrent runs are different quantities. No numeric bound or derivation is given.

AC3's 'tested tip == the landed tree' has no defined guard against state changing between assembly, CI completion and submit. Three things can change mid-flight: main can advance; an author can upload a new patchset; an author can remove the Autosubmit vote or abandon a change. Submitting after green is a check-then-act (TOCTOU) unless the plan requires a compare-and-set.

The batch-size bound is unquantified. It also mixes units: 'one CI run's job budget' versus 'GHA concurrency cap (~3 concurrent runs)'. Since a batch is always one CI run regardless of size, it is unclear what the bound actually limits. Behaviour when more changes are queued than the bound allows is also unspecified.

AC1 assumes queued, independent stacks can be put into 'one combined linear chain' with no side effects. Doing this means re-parenting each stack onto the previous stack's tip, which uploads new patch sets to other authors' changes. Whether Autosubmit and Code-Review votes carry over to those patch sets depends on each label's copyCondition (e.g., changekind:TRIVIAL_REBASE). The plan doesn't check this. Gerrit's rebase:chain endpoint only works on one linear ancestry chain and doesn't combine separate stacks.

AC1 assumes independent queued stacks can be re-parented into one linear chain without losing submit eligibility. Re-parenting creates new patch sets, and whether Code-Review and Autosubmit votes carry over depends on Gerrit label copy conditions (copyCondition / copyAllScoresOnTrivialRebase), which the plan does not state and the repo does not contain.

Assembling independent changes into 'ONE combined linear chain' means rebasing or re-parenting other authors' changes, which creates new Gerrit patchsets on each one. The plan does not account for (a) Code-Review/Verified votes being reset on the new patchsets, which depends on label copy rules and can leave the chain unsubmittable; (b) rebase conflicts when a later stack does not apply cleanly on an earlier one; or (c) who is recorded as the patchset uploader. Without these, the assembly step can fail or produce a chain that cannot be submitted, even with green CI.

The plan does not say how independent stacks become 'one combined linear chain' or what happens when doing so hits a conflict. Building the chain requires rebasing each stack onto the previous stack's tip, which can produce merge conflicts. Batch-failure handling is declared out of scope, but an assembly-time conflict is not a CI failure, so it falls inside this story and is unhandled.

AC3's 'on green, submits' implicitly needs a Verified (CI) vote on the batch changes so Gerrit will let them submit. The plan moves 'Verified-casting' to a separate, uncited story, so it is unconfirmed that anything casts the vote this plan's submit step needs.

The plan assumes a single CI run on the combined tip lets the whole batch land atomically. In Gerrit, submitting the tip of a relation chain only submits ancestors that are themselves submittable. Each ancestor change must meet its own submit requirements (e.g. Verified+1, Code-Review+2). One CI run on the tip does not vote on the ancestors, and 'Verified-casting' is explicitly out of scope. So AC3 depends on a capability that this phase excludes and that hasn't been verified.

AC2 'exactly ONE CI run' contradicts AC3's re-assemble/re-batch loop, and the re-check timing is unclear: AC3 says that if main has advanced, the batch is re-assembled and re-batched up to N=5 times. A re-assembled chain is a new tree with a new tip SHA, so it needs a new CI dispatch, a new run_id and a new tested_sha. That breaks AC2's literal 'exactly ONE CI run on the combined tip' and the Why section's '~1 CI cycle' claim. The worst case is 6 runs. AC3 also places the re-check 'immediately before the batch is handed off for submit', which is after green. Re-assembling at that point throws away the green result. The plan never says whether the in-flight or finished run_id/tested_sha is replaced, or whether a superseded run is cancelled. An implementer cannot meet both ACs as written.

Serial fallback gets a rewritten, coupled chain, not the original independent stacks: By the time the batch is dropped to the Phase-1 serial path, assembly has already rebased every member into one linear relation chain, so members from unrelated stacks are now ancestors of each other in Gerrit. The plan does not restore each stack's original parentage. The serial lander would see one long stack, and a failure in one member would block unrelated members. The fallback that is supposed to guarantee progress would keep the batch coupled.

Building cross-stack chains with /rebase:chain is asserted but not grounded: AC1 assumes S2's `/rebase:chain` is 'the building block for cross-stack chain assembly'. Gerrit's rebase:chain rebases one existing ancestry chain. Joining N independent stacks means re-parenting stack B's root onto stack A's tip. The plan does not show that this endpoint can do that, or that per-root rebase with an explicit base is needed instead. No Gerrit client code exists in the repo to check against, and the S2 ticket that supposedly provides this machinery cannot be found. The core mechanism of the story is unproven.

Rebase conflicts during assembly are not handled: The What section says 'combine N non-conflicting changes', but no AC says how non-conflict is decided or what happens when rebasing member k onto the partial chain conflicts. The plan defers batch failure handling to S9, but S9 covers failures after CI. A conflict during assembly happens before any CI run, so it is S7's problem. Without a rule the executor cannot tell whether to drop the conflicting member and continue, abort the whole batch, or fall back to serial. An abandoned partial chain would also leave members rebased onto unrelated parents.

Batch-state store for the S7→S8 handoff is undefined, and the record lacks the base SHA: S8 depends on a 'batch state' record, but the plan never says where it lives, who may write it, when it is created or invalidated, or what happens to it after re-batch or fallback. The record also omits the main base SHA the chain was assembled on. Without that, S8 cannot independently confirm that the tested tree is still on current main, so it has to trust S7's TOCTOU check blindly. If parties other than the lander can write the store, a forged record could make S8 cast Verified on untested code.

BATCH_MAX=8 rationale contradicts the plan's own CI model: The cap is justified as 'sized to one run's job budget under the GHA concurrency cap'. But the plan triggers one run per batch, so the job count does not grow with the number of members. The Why section also says the concurrent-run count 'isn't the limiter'. No measurement leads to the number 8. The real tradeoff is how much work a failed batch throws away and how much S9 has to bisect, and the plan never states it.

gerrit-verify.yaml and its concurrency-group and dispatch-input premises are unverified: The plan relies on gerrit-verify.yaml having a per-change concurrency group and accepting dispatch against a given change number and patchset. The repo has no such workflow; a search finds the name only in the review cache. The plan does not say whether S7 must add a workflow_dispatch trigger with these inputs, or which ticket creates the workflow. It also ignores that a per-change concurrency group keyed on the combined-tip change could cancel or queue runs when a re-batch re-dispatches on the same change.

No testing plan for assembly, the re-batch bound, or the fallback: The plan has no test or verification AC. Its riskiest behaviors have no stated way to show they work: multi-stack chain assembly, the N=5 bounded loop ending in serial fallback, BATCH_MAX enforcement with excess changes deferred, and single-dispatch-per-tree. The ACs are written as behaviors with no evidence kind.

The bounded re-batch loop implies up to N=5 additional CI runs and CI cycles. That contradicts AC2's 'exactly ONE CI run on the combined tip' and the Why section's claim that batching 'collapses it to ~1 CI cycle'. The plan also does not say whether the main-tip re-check happens before CI dispatch or after green. After green, any re-assembly invalidates tested_sha and needs a fresh run.

The plan does not say how a single queued stack with more than BATCH_MAX changes is handled. Its changes cannot be split across batches without breaking ancestry. It also does not say whether 'members' counts changes or stacks.

The AC 'Triggers exactly ONE CI run on the combined tip' contradicts the FFO re-batch loop. Each re-assembly onto a new main tip produces a new combined tip and tested_sha, so it needs a fresh CI run. The plan never says whether re-batch re-dispatches CI or how many runs a batch may consume.

Falling back to the Phase-1 serial path after N=5 failed re-batches doesn't work as written. By then /rebase:chain has given every member a new patchset and a new parent, so the members are one linear relation chain in Gerrit. The serial lander will see one N-member stack, not N independent stacks. It would land them all-or-nothing as a single stack, which is just an untested-for-current-main batch under another name. Each original stack has to be split back out (rebased onto main again on its own) before handing it to the serial path.

Nothing covers a merge conflict during assembly. The algorithm is described as combining 'N non-conflicting changes', but no AC says how non-conflicting members are picked or what happens when /rebase:chain fails partway through for one member: skip it and continue, abort the batch, or roll back the members already rebased. CI-failure handling belongs to S9, but an assembly-time conflict happens inside S7.

The plan never says what happens when assembly hits a rebase conflict. It says to combine 'non-conflicting' changes, but not how a conflicting member or stack is detected and handled: excluded and left queued, whole stack excluded, or whole batch aborted. Member ordering within the combined chain is also unspecified (queue/FIFO order, submit-order timestamp, etc.).

Assembly-time failures are unhandled. If /rebase:chain hits a merge conflict or Gerrit error on member k, earlier members have already received new rebased patchsets. The plan does not define the policy: exclude the conflicting member and continue, or abort and leave members rebased. 'non-conflicting' is assumed, not enforced.

The handoff record is under-specified. The plan never says where 'batch state' is persisted or what its schema/ownership is. The record also lacks each member's tested patchset/revision SHA and the base main SHA. Without these, S8 cannot bind each Verified vote to the exact member patchset that was tested, or re-check that main hasn't advanced in the window between S7's re-check and S8's submit.

The handoff record carries only the tip's tested_sha, not each member's tested patchset number or revision SHA. Gerrit votes are cast per member revision, so S8 cannot verify that the member patchset it votes on is the one assembled and tested.

The BATCH_MAX=8 cap interacts undefinedly with stacks. A relation chain longer than 8 can never fit and may starve, and the selection order for which ≤8 members join a batch is unspecified. The rationale 'sized to one run's job budget' is also unclear, since a single combined-tip run's job count does not obviously scale with member count.

AC2 says S7 records the dispatched run's `run_id` on the batch, but the plan doesn't say how the run_id is obtained. GitHub's `POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/workflows/{workflow}/dispatches` has historically returned 204 No Content with no run id. Correlating the dispatch to its run requires polling `GET .../actions/runs` filtered by event/created time plus a unique correlation input, or a response option the plan hasn't checked is available.

The positive rationale in ## Why contradicts itself. It says speculation 'would just queue' under the concurrency cap, then says 'the exact concurrent-run count isn't the limiter' because gerrit-verify.yaml uses a per-change concurrency group. A per-change group means runs on different changes do not block each other, which argues for speculation, not against it. Batching may still be the better choice, but the reason given doesn't establish it, and the S9 failure-recovery design will depend on it.

BATCH_MAX=8 is justified as 'sized to one run's job budget under the GHA concurrency cap'. The Why section says the concurrency count is not the limiter. 'Job budget' is never defined, and the number 8 is asserted rather than derived.

Assembly re-parents independent stacks onto each other, creating new patchsets on authors' changes and a cross-stack relation chain. The plan gives no back-out for when a batch is abandoned: dropped to serial after N=5, or excluded on conflict. Members may stay chained to unrelated stacks, so the Phase-1 serial path would land them as one chain. The plan also gives no rollout or kill switch for switching the lander from serial to batching.

The batch-state handoff record has no defined lifecycle. Undefined points: creation time (per attempt or per batch), behavior on re-batch (overwrite, version, or append), how S8 tells a superseded record from the current one, and retirement after submit, after drop-to-serial, or on S9 failure handling.

The plan builds the batch from the real member changes, not a staging/synthetic ref, and states this as a requirement without justification. bors, Zuul and GitHub merge queue all test on a staging or speculative ref so the changes under review are not modified. Here, assembly uploads new patchsets onto every member change and re-parents each stack onto unrelated queued changes. If the batch fails or is dropped, members stay chained to unrelated work, may lose votes depending on copy rules, and S9 must unwind the relation chains. The plan gives no reason for this break from the established pattern.

`BATCH_MAX=8` is described as 'sized to one run's job budget under the GHA concurrency cap', but the plan gives no derivation, and it conflicts with the plan's own reasoning. The Why says the concurrent-run count 'isn't the limiter', and the whole design runs exactly ONE CI run whatever N is, so the jobs per run shouldn't grow with the number of members. GitHub Free allows 20 concurrent jobs per account, which doesn't lead to 8. The established batching tradeoff (bors: batch size against bisection cost when batches fail) isn't cited as the basis either.

The reason given for BATCH_MAX=8 doesn't match the plan's own model of CI, so the number looks like a cap copied from batching tools without an evidenced basis (cargo-cult / premature-optimization). The plan says one batch fires ONE `gerrit-verify.yaml` run on the combined tip, so the job count shouldn't grow with the number of members. The Why section also says 'the exact concurrent-run count isn't the limiter'. Yet the cap is justified as 'sized to one run's job budget under the GHA concurrency cap', and the plan gives no job count, timing or other measurement that would produce 8.

Rebasing N members creates N new patchsets. If gerrit-verify.yaml (or the S2 machinery) is also triggered by patchset-created events, assembly would launch one run per member, violating 'exactly ONE CI run'. The plan does not say how per-member auto-triggers are suppressed during batch assembly.

Two of the five targets are already behavioral tests, so the inventory is out of date: The plan says its inventory is 'VALIDATED', but two of its five targets no longer exist in the anti-pattern form it describes. Index-keyed chunks need a unit order that is the same in every xdist worker: Each xdist worker collects on its own. xdist checks only that node ids match across workers. With ids like chunk index k, it can't tell if chunk k holds different units on different workers. If _renderable_units() lists the corpus in an order that isn't fixed (unsorted listdir/glob), units can be duplicated or skipped across workers while each worker's guard still passes.

'Bounded by construction' caps the number of units per chunk, not the time a chunk takes: A fixed chunk of 40 units limits how many units a chunk holds, not how long it runs, because pandoc time scales with each unit's size. If large fixtures are added and land in one chunk, that chunk can still go past the ~10s idle bound or the 300s load budget. So the claim that the failure 'can never be re-crossed by fixture growth' is overstated.

In that case gw0's chunk 3 and gw1's chunk 3 contain different units: some units get compared twice and some never. The coverage guard runs in a single process and would not notice.

`_renderable_units()` is computed at module import and sliced into index-keyed parametrize cases. If enumeration depends on filesystem/glob order, chunk `[k]` can hold different units on different workers. That would silently duplicate some units and skip others, while each worker's own coverage guard still passes.

The chunked design assumes `_renderable_units()` returns the same order in every xdist worker process, but the plan never requires this. Each worker imports the module and recomputes the list itself, and parametrize IDs are keyed only by chunk index. If the order ever differs between processes (for example an unsorted directory walk or glob, or set iteration), xdist's check that workers collected the same IDs still passes because the IDs match. But chunk N would hold different units on different workers, so some units are compared twice and others never. The new coverage guard runs in a single process and cannot detect this.
